title: Moon Mission Makeover: Astronauts Will Test Space Docking, Not Walk on the Moon!
summary: Imagine training for the biggest race of your life, but then the finish line gets moved—to a completely different track! That's kind of what just happened to four astronauts. NASA picked the crew for Artemis III, a mission that was supposed to put the first people on the Moon since 1972. But now, they won't even go near it. Instead, they'll stay in low Earth orbit, about the same height as the International Space Station, and practice connecting their spaceship to Moon landers. Commander Randy Bresnik will lead the team. Italian astronaut Luca Parmitano, who has spent over 300 days in space, will be the pilot. Americans Andre Douglas and Frank Rubio are the mission specialists, and Bob Heintz is the backup—he can fill any role if needed. So why the big change? The giant Starship rocket from SpaceX, meant to carry astronauts to the Moon's surface, isn't ready. It's so heavy it needs to refuel in space, a tricky move never tested before. Plus, Blue Origin's New Glenn rocket blew up during a test last month, damaging the launch pad badly. That delays other Moon landers. NASA still hopes Artemis III will fly in 2027 as a test, with a real landing in 2028. But many experts think that timeline is super ambitious—like trying to finish a year's worth of homework in one night!
why_it_matters: It shows that even big plans can change, and scientists must be patient and solve problems step by step — just like when you practice before a big game or test.

background_read: The last time people walked on the Moon was in 1972 during the Apollo 17 mission. Since then, only robots have visited the lunar surface.
Astronauts often practice connecting to other spacecraft in low Earth orbit, near the International Space Station (a giant floating laboratory).
SpaceX (Elon Musk's rocket company) and Blue Origin (Jeff Bezos's space company) are both building Moon landers, but the technology is very new and has hit delays.
Article_Structure: WHO: The Artemis III crew — commander Randy Bresnik, pilot Luca Parmitano, mission specialists Andre Douglas and Frank Rubio, and backup Bob Heintz.
WHAT: Their mission changed from landing on the Moon to practicing docking with Moon landers in low Earth orbit.
WHERE: In low Earth orbit, about the same height as the International Space Station.
WHY: The Starship rocket isn't ready and must test refueling in space; a Blue Origin rocket explosion also delayed other landers.

perspectives.description: Some people feel excited that astronauts will test new docking skills, which will make future Moon landings safer for everyone.
Others are disappointed because they hoped to see new Moon walks soon, and delays might mean younger astronauts get the chance instead.
Experts see this as a wise change to avoid dangerous failures, even if it means waiting longer for a real landing.
